lines.text: Iron makes heliodor gold and aquamarine blue.
lines.say: Iron makes HEE-lee-oh-dor gold and AK-wuh-muh-REEN blue.

lines.text: Heliodor and aquamarine are beryl, the same mineral as emerald.
lines.say: HEE-lee-oh-dor and AK-wuh-muh-REEN are BAIR-ul, the same mineral as EM-rald.

lines.text: Pure beryl is colorless, and tiny traces add the colors.
lines.say: Pure BAIR-ul is colorless, and tiny traces add the colors.

lines.text: Emerald gets its green from chromium or vanadium.
lines.say: EM-rald gets its green from KROH-mee-um or vuh-NAY-dee-um.

lines.say: HEE-lee-oh-dor is often found in the same deposits as AK-wuh-muh-REEN.

post.caption: Iron makes heliodor gold and aquamarine blue. Heliodor and aquamarine are beryl, the same mineral as emerald. Pure beryl is colorless, and tiny traces add the colors. Emerald gets its green from chromium or vanadium. Iron colors heliodor a golden yellow. Iron colors aquamarine blue too, so one element paints both stones. The name comes from Greek words meaning gift of the sun. It began as a trade name for yellow beryl from Namibia. Heliodor is often found in the same deposits as aquamarine. Heat can turn some yellow beryl blue. Heliodor rates about 7.5 to 8 on the Mohs hardness scale.
